mission: Coordinate peripheral metabolic clock timing through feeding cues.

stage2a.operation: Feeding-related peripheral entrainment is distinct from retinal central-clock entrainment. Reuse bounded phase evidence; do not convert a phase shift into a beneficial dietary effect.

existing_findings.proposition: In ten healthy men, a five-hour meal delay shifted glucose rhythm timing by 5.69 ± 1.29 hours and adipose PER2 by 0.97 ± 0.29 hours, without significant changes in measured melatonin or cortisol timing.

existing_source_assessments.label: Wehrens et al. (2017)
existing_source_assessments.directional_finding: Glucose and adipose PER2 timing shifted, while melatonin and cortisol timing did not.

assessment.study: Ten healthy men; meals five hours apart, starting 0.5 versus 5.5 hours after waking; 37-hour constant-routine rhythm assessments.
assessment.result: In ten healthy men, a five-hour meal delay shifted glucose rhythm timing by 5.69 ± 1.29 hours and adipose PER2 by 0.97 ± 0.29 hours, without significant changes in measured melatonin or cortisol timing.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Glucose phase +5.69 ± 1.29 h; adipose PER2 +0.97 ± 0.29 h; these are measured responses, not the five-hour exposure dose.
assessment.evidence_summary: Meal timing changed peripheral metabolic and adipose-clock readouts without moving the measured central hormonal timing.
assessment.limitations: Small ordered rather than randomised sequence; peripheral clock-gene sampling, not direct SCN recording. No optimum eating window or clinical benefit established.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Full primary Results/Methods retrieved; Figure 2 glucose and Figure 4 adipose clock-gene analysis.

existing_supportive_evidence.label: Hatori et al. (2012)
existing_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Time-restricted feeding without a calorie reduction prevented metabolic disease in mice on a high-fat diet.
existing_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: Metabolic protection is not a measurement of peripheral clock phase in humans.

existing_supportive_evidence.label: Garaulet and Gómez-Abellán (2014)
existing_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: The review associates the timing of food intake with obesity.
existing_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: An association with obesity does not establish that a peripheral clock moved.

existing_findings.disposition: Existing canonical assessment retained; enrichment is additive. No clinical or source-level negative inferred from bounded retrieval.

existing_findings.proposition: Animal feeding manipulations shift peripheral clock rhythms while central-clock phase remains linked to the light cycle.

existing_source_assessments.label: Stokkan et al. (2001)
existing_source_assessments.directional_finding: Liver rhythm shifted by approximately ten hours within two days while SCN rhythmicity stayed phase-locked to the light–dark cycle.

assessment.study: Transgenic rat tissue rhythms under restricted feeding.
assessment.population: Transgenic rat tissue rhythms under restricted feeding.
assessment.result: Liver rhythm shifted by approximately ten hours within two days while SCN rhythmicity stayed phase-locked to the light–dark cycle.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Liver rhythm shifted by approximately ten hours within two days while SCN rhythmicity stayed phase-locked to the light–dark cycle.
assessment.evidence_summary: Liver rhythm shifted by approximately ten hours within two days while SCN rhythmicity stayed phase-locked to the light–dark cycle.
assessment.limitations: Animal liver entrainment, not a human optimum meal schedule.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary abstract retrieved; no unextracted full-method detail asserted.

existing_source_assessments.label: Damiola et al. (2000)
existing_source_assessments.directional_finding: Peripheral gene-expression phase shifted by up to twelve hours while SCN phase remained unaffected; adaptation differed across tissues.

assessment.study: Mouse daytime/night-time restricted feeding with peripheral and SCN clock-gene measurements.
assessment.population: Mouse daytime/night-time restricted feeding with peripheral and SCN clock-gene measurements.
assessment.result: Peripheral gene-expression phase shifted by up to twelve hours while SCN phase remained unaffected; adaptation differed across tissues.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Peripheral gene-expression phase shifted by up to twelve hours while SCN phase remained unaffected; adaptation differed across tissues.
assessment.evidence_summary: Peripheral gene-expression phase shifted by up to twelve hours while SCN phase remained unaffected; adaptation differed across tissues.
assessment.limitations: Peripheral uncoupling can occur; a shift is not proof of beneficial alignment.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary abstract retrieved; no unextracted full-method detail asserted.

existing_source_assessments.label: Crosby et al. (2019)
existing_source_assessments.directional_finding: Insulin/IGF-1 induced PERIOD proteins and reset rhythms; mistimed signalling disrupted circadian organisation.

assessment.study: Cellular and mouse insulin/IGF-1 signalling manipulations.
assessment.population: Cellular and mouse insulin/IGF-1 signalling manipulations.
assessment.result: Insulin/IGF-1 induced PERIOD proteins and reset rhythms; mistimed signalling disrupted circadian organisation.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Insulin/IGF-1 induced PERIOD proteins and reset rhythms; mistimed signalling disrupted circadian organisation.
assessment.evidence_summary: Insulin/IGF-1 induced PERIOD proteins and reset rhythms; mistimed signalling disrupted circadian organisation.
assessment.limitations: Animal/cellular mechanism, not proof that a particular human diet optimises clocks.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary abstract retrieved; no unextracted full-method detail asserted.

existing_findings.disposition: Existing canonical assessment retained; enrichment is additive. No clinical or source-level negative inferred from bounded retrieval.

stage2a.evidence_enrichment: Human meal-delay effects on glucose and adipose PER2 phase differ from melatonin/cortisol phase and from a demonstrated health improvement. Animal insulin/clock experiments remain contextual and do not create extra human replications.

source_to_claim_records.proposition: A five-hour meal delay shifted glucose and adipose PER2 rhythms without shifting melatonin or cortisol rhythms.
source_to_claim_records.limitation: Ten healthy young men in ordered laboratory schedules; phase shifts are not proof of improved health or a prescription for an optimum clock time.
source_to_claim_records.retrieval: Primary paper abstract/results and existing source assessment compared; full methods where accessible.

stage2a.coverage_limitations: Existing source assessments and full attached bibliography are inventoried and preserved. Targeted source retrieval is bounded to the stated propositions; unrefreshed clinical/Phenome sources are not newly validated. No evidence of absence is inferred.
stage2a.stop_rationale: Preserve the complete baseline, add the bounded supported evidence and exact qualifications, and park material attribution/traceability questions for approval instead of forcing an admission or expanding to a comprehensive rebuild.

stage2b.clarification: The existing meal-schedule SOP is retained. Peripheral clock timing is distinct from retinal light entrainment; no extra dietary substance, preferred universal meal time or clinical efficacy claim is added.

existing_practices.biological_role: Meal timing can shift peripheral glucose and adipose clock-gene rhythms while measured melatonin and cortisol timing remain unchanged.
existing_practices.evidence_limitation: Five-hour meal delay in ten healthy men; PER2 shifted about one hour. No universal eating window, improved alignment or health benefit is established.
existing_practices.reader_description: Meal timing can shift peripheral glucose and adipose clock-gene rhythms while measured melatonin and cortisol timing remain unchanged.
